title: Blanche’s Confirmation Vote Could Flip the Senate
author: Nick Licata
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Todd_Blanche_Sworn_In_As_AG-680x453.jpg)

Photograph Source: From X (Twitter) - Public Domain

The Epstein files are the Achilles’ heel for Republican Senators this
November, and their vote to confirm Todd Blanche as U.S. Attorney General is
the Democrats’ populist arrow that could topple them.

**Populist-oriented voters are up for grabs.**

Although polls have repeatedly shown that most voters believe there is a
wealth gap between them and the top 1% (_see[Congress Can Reverse America’s
Growing Wealth Disparity](https://us.list-
manage.com/Kmog1V06yPa?e=c1b0f52ff1&c2id=cac44224e2f228c427dd633f05ac899f)_),
that is only the tip of the iceberg of their dissatisfaction with our society.
Many see America as ruled by an elite that disrespects them. As recently as
2024, an Ipsos Global Advisor survey found that 69% of Americans believe the
political and economic elite don't care about hard-working people.

Democrats don’t realize that a large swath of Republican and conservative
independent voters care about the elite class getting away with escapades that
would land any of them in jail. They have a populist attitude about exposing
this elite class for being above common decency, more so than compensating the
Capitol Hill insurrectionists or allowing Trump and his family an exemption
from paying their taxes.

Populist discontent among Republicans and conservative independents is evident
in polls about the release of all government files related to Epstein. A
PBS/NPR/Marist poll found that about two-thirds of Republicans (67%) wanted
all the Epstein files released, and a separate YouGov survey found 73–80% of
Republicans wanted the same.

The Epstein files are different for the Republican supporter base like no
other issue because they reflect a basic populist tenet that political and
economic elites operate under different social norms than everyone else. It is
not a partisan issue; it’s about not trusting government to treat elites the
same as everyone else, and it is not so much about detailed policy issues.

Senate Republicans' vote to confirm Blanche as the Attorney General opens the
door for Democrats to address the concerns of 53% of Republican voters.
According to the YouGov survey, these voters believe the government is
covering up evidence about Epstein to protect the elites.

**Democrats’ campaigns are not reaching out to disaffected populists.**

Although Senate Democrats note that Blanche refused to release all the Epstein
Files, they are not treating it as a campaign issue to attract the populist
base they critically need to win elections. The closest Democrats come to
capturing the populist spirit that sustains the MAGA movement is to call for a
fair tax on the rich. But Democrats have been banging that drum for years, and
nothing has changed. Democrats running for Congress must open their eyes and
minds to the fact that the Epstein Files are the soft underbelly of Republican
candidates because Republicans are keeping them from the public.

Instead, Democrats have focused on objecting to Blanche over two main issues.
First, his role in the IRS tax-audit settlement that grants special audit
protections to Trump and retroactivity for his Trump-affiliated businesses.
Second, his role in providing a $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" payout fund
for Trump allies.

Democrats don’t realize that a large swath of Republican and conservative
independent voters care about the elite class getting away with escapades that
would land any of them in jail. They care more about exposing an elite class
for being above common decency than about compensating the Capitol
insurrectionists or granting Trump and his family an exemption from paying
their taxes.

What will motivate these voters is not to allow elites to flaunt their
immunity from being called out for violating the most vulnerable in their
community, young girls who are used and then tossed aside by old white men.

**Senate machinations will force an early vote to confirm Blanche.**

Senators John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) capitulated to
President Donald Trump’s demand that Blanche be confirmed immediately. With
the Senate scheduled to leave the Capitol on Monday or soon after, the
confirmation vote must occur before then. That leaves little to no time to
persuade Republicans to vote against or abstain from Blanche’s confirmation.

Cornyn and Tillis claimed victory in stopping the payout fund by getting
Blanche to write a memo stating he would not have the DOJ pursue it, though he
could later rationalize doing so. However, Cornyn and Tillis are now
supporting Blanche without pushing to drop the IRS tax-audit settlement. And
they have stopped talking about the Epstein Files.

Cornyn and Tillis are leaving open seats because they will not be running for
office in November. They had been expected to be easily won by another
Republican. However, the Cook Political Report classified both seats as
trending toward a Democratic advantage. There is some restlessness among
voters for meaningful change. This is an opportunity to reach out to those who
would not normally vote for a Democrat.

**Blanche is the poster child for protecting a corrupt elite.**

Democrats have not highlighted that Republican Senators are protecting
powerful men who were guests of Jeffrey Epstein, who was convicted of
soliciting prostitution and procuring minors for prostitution. Blanche is
directly responsible for hiding the Epstein files from the public. A vote to
confirm him is a vote to keep the files hidden from the public to protect the
rich and powerful.

Former Attorney General Pam Bondi told the House Oversight Committee that
then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche was "in charge of the process and
the entire release of the Epstein files." In effect, he directed redaction
training and privilege determinations regarding who should not be disclosed as
an Epstein guest.

Congress was under intense pressure from both left- and right-wing voters,
leading to the passage of the Epstein Files Transparency Act (H.R. 4405), with
only 1 dissenting vote in the House and unanimous passage in the Senate. The
law required the U.S. Attorney General to make all unclassified Department of
Justice records, communications, and investigative materials publicly
available in a searchable, downloadable format.

According to senior United States District Judge Emmet G. Sullivan (appointed
to the District of Columbia Court of Appeals in 1992 by George H.W. Bush), the
DOJ has ignored the express intent of this requirement. This past month, Judge
Sullivan ordered the DOJ to turn over unredacted or less redacted versions of
the Epstein files, rejecting the department's arguments for secrecy. Sullivan
also concluded that Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche essentially admitted
violating the Epstein Files Transparency Act by failing to address allegations
from independent journalist Katie Phang in a lawsuit seeking broader access to
the records.

What we have here is more than just “a failure to communicate.” We have direct
obstruction of a law that every member of Congress, except one, voted for.
Voting to confirm Todd Blanche allows an elite class of wealthy and
influential men to avoid recognition and possible indictment based on what is
currently in the Epstein files.

Members who vote to confirm Blanche are guilty of obstructing the law, not to
comfort the weak or average citizen, but to protect our most elite class of
citizens. It appears that all but one or two Republicans will vote to bury the
Epstein files by confirming Blanche, who has already acted to do so.

What can Democrats do about it? They can make it a populist campaign issue to
throw the scoundrels out for violating the law and family values.

**Control of the Senate comes down to appealing to populist voters**

**If the Republicans lose 4 or more seats** and the Democrats lose no seats,
the Democrats will take a majority control of the Senate. Democrats have been
running on a range of issues, from social justice to affordability, many of
which also link to Trump’s corruption and his Iran War. But they have largely
ignored campaigning on the issue of the Epstein files.

If the Senate is to have a Democratic majority, it must reach out to voters
who would abandon support for the Republican candidates if it were made clear
that those Republicans are siding with the carefree values of the elites, not
with those held by an average citizen’s sense of responsibility to the
community.

Unfortunately, none of the campaign websites for the following Democratic
Senate candidates, whether challenging vulnerable incumbent Senators or
running for open seats, mention the Epstein Files:

> Alaska - Mary Peltola
>
> Iowa - Josh Turek
>
> Maine - Troy Jackson
>
> Michigan - Abdul El-Sayed
>
> North Carolina - Roy Cooper
>
> Ohio - Sherrod Brown
>
> Texas - James Talarico
>
> Utah - John Curtis

When Graham Platner was a Senate candidate, he made the release of the Epstein
files a central theme of his campaign. As of today, his replacement, Troy
Jackson, has not pursued that issue.

Although Democratic Senate candidates have not used the Epstein files to reach
out to disaffected Republicans or conservative independents, Democrats and
allies of some of those candidates have done so on their behalf. In Iowa,
incumbent Republican Senator Ashley Hinson was attacked for her initial
opposition to releasing the files. Democrats supporting Ohio’s Sherrod Brown
have run ads tying Republicans to what they call the "Epstein class."

However, none of these candidates have matched Georgia incumbent Senator Jon
Ossoff’s level of engagement on this issue. At campaign rallies, he has
referred to "the Epstein class" as a symbol of wealthy elites receiving
special treatment and has repeatedly called for full disclosure of the files.

Republicans’ biggest Super PACs plan to spend $40 million to unseat Ossoff
because he consistently leads Republican challenger Representative Mike
Collins. Ossoff’s populist emphasis on tying Republicans to defending an
Epstein class appears to be appealing to voters who have supported Trump in
the past, as he is the only Democrat running for reelection in a state Donald
Trump carried in 2024.

**Bottom Line**

If the Democrats wish to win enough seats to become the majority in the
Senate, they cannot rely solely on voters who have often heard their promises
of greater social justice and economic opportunities. Those issues will
generate support from their base, but they are not a sufficiently populist
message to attract new voters. If candidates like Abdul El-Sayed and Troy
Jackson run as progressives or as populists, they need to go beyond appealing
to liberal voters.

They need to feel the pent-up anger that many working people have toward a
system that has failed to meet the expectations Democrats have repeatedly
offered. Democratic candidates don’t seem to understand that offering good
policies backed by data and logical solutions doesn’t address the gut feeling
many voters have of being disrespected by an elite that appears to run this
country.

Democrats need to attract voters who feel abandoned by the Republicans. If the
Democrats are to appeal to them, they must recognize that this country has a
significant social divide between the wealthy and wage earners. And it is a
cultural divide, even more so than a divide of wealth.

The Epstein files revealed the cultural divide more than any other event in
the past decade. Any senator who voted to confirm Todd Blanche was voting to
shield an elite from accountability in our justice system, which applies to
all of us. That is the populist message the Democrats need to send.
